content: The evidence base for healthcare-associated infections (HCAI) in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) remains limited. Studies of lower quality, identified in a scoping review, consistently reported protective effects of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions. However, these studies are often confounded by other factors. While ensuring safe and adequate WASH in healthcare facilities is a clear public health priority and a human rights issue, further research in LMICs is essential to strengthen policies, improve programmatic responses, and support investments in more effective and efficient interventions. Collaboration between health, environmental health, local government, and finance ministries is critical to achieving universal access to quality care. However, monitoring efforts for WASH in healthcare facilities have been inadequate. Until recently, only a few national health monitoring systems collected meaningful data on WASH in healthcare settings, with most data coming from externally conducted facility assessments. Without reliable data on the quality of WASH services, disaggregated by facility type and location, it has been challenging to identify needs, respond effectively, and develop costed improvement plans. The 2015 WHO/UNICEF report on WASH in healthcare facilities analyzed data from over 54,000 facilities, while the 2019 Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) report expanded this to over 560,000 facilities. Using the JMP framework for monitoring WASH in healthcare facilities is expected to significantly enhance data collection and analysis. National health budgets are often organized by disease-specific areas, with line items for routine costs like vaccines and medicines, rather than cross-cutting health system functions such as WASH. As a result, healthcare facilities frequently lack funds for capital infrastructure investments, ongoing operations, maintenance, and overlooked functions like cleaning and waste management. Decentralized budgeting in many countries has not been accompanied by sufficient local revenue schemes to generate funds for WASH, particularly in rural areas. Healthcare facility staff are often overburdened and lack the training or incentives to improve and manage WASH services. Facility administrators, healthcare providers, and patients frequently view inadequate WASH as an intractable issue, especially when improvements are perceived to require costly infrastructure upgrades. Many low-income countries and underserved areas within middle-income countries lack fully functioning, safely managed municipal water and sanitation services. In such cases, healthcare facilities may require significant capital investments that exceed available health budgets. Addressing these challenges will require effective intersectoral collaboration, particularly to tackle issues like antimicrobial resistance (AMR), where poor WASH in healthcare facilities contributes to preventable infections and environmental contamination with resistant pathogens. Since 2015, WHO, UNICEF, and other partners have worked together to improve WASH in healthcare facilities. Progress has been made in embedding WASH standards into global health documents and advocating for practical steps at the national level. Over 35 partners, including UN agencies, have committed to improving WASH in healthcare facilities. However, achieving universal access to WASH in healthcare facilities requires leadership and action-focused commitments at international, regional, national, and local levels. Strong institutional leadership from ministries of health, water, sanitation, and finance, as well as local governments, is essential for coordinated efforts. The Ethiopian government launched the Clean and Safe Health Facility (CASH) initiative in 2014 to improve cleanliness in healthcare facilities, reduce healthcare-associated infections, and enhance patient safety. This initiative, driven by government leadership, has been implemented in all 150 national hospitals and is now expanding to primary healthcare facilities. Community engagement, private sector involvement, and high-level leadership have been critical to its success. Challenges include scaling the program to thousands of health centers and posts and ensuring sustainable funding from regular budgets. In Cambodia, a situation analysis conducted in 2015 identified WASH as a priority for improving quality of care. This analysis informed the development of new WASH guidelines, integration of WASH into health management training, and the use of tools like WASH FIT to monitor and improve services. Operational research on hygiene behavior and IPC practices during childbirth is ongoing. Continuous updates to health system analyses and flexible funding have been essential for influencing policy and scaling evidence-based actions. Ghana has made significant progress in improving WASH in healthcare facilities by establishing national standards, integrating WASH into IPC programs, and aligning efforts with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A national strategy for WASH in healthcare facilities has been developed, with most improvements financed through domestic resources. Challenges include coordinating efforts among multiple stakeholders and addressing underfunded areas like healthcare waste management. Low-cost WASH interventions, such as portable handwashing and drinking water stations, have been shown to rapidly reduce healthcare-associated infections in rural Kenyan facilities. These interventions serve as effective interim solutions while more sustainable WASH services are planned and implemented. National standards and policies for WASH in healthcare facilities are essential for implementation, monitoring, and regulation. These standards should be comprehensive, actionable, and context-specific, addressing the needs of vulnerable populations. Once established, WASH standards should be integrated into quality of care guidelines, IPC strategies, and national health policies.
